merge_reason: Kept separate because this is a distinct diagnostic nephrology investigation of pseudo-Bartter physiology and its differential, including verification of any lipedema-specific cases.
prompt: Conduct a narrowly focused nephrology/diagnostic investigation of pseudo-Bartter-like physiology and differential diagnosis in a person with lipedema, not a general audit of diuretic indications. Define the biochemical phenotype—hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia, metabolic alkalosis, volume contraction and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system—and distinguish it from Bartter and Gitelman syndromes; vomiting or nasogastric suction; chloride-losing diarrhoea or congenital chloride diarrhoea; cystic-fibrosis-related losses; severe sweating; laxative-associated disorders; surreptitious or prescribed diuretic exposure; adrenal or mineralocorticoid excess; renal tubular disease; and acetazolamide-related metabolic acidosis. Examine interpretation of urine chloride and potassium, timing relative to the last diuretic dose and sample handling, limitations of diuretic screening including panel coverage, sensitivity, false negatives and detection window, relevant acid-base, electrolyte and renal tests, and urgent symptoms. Specifically search for and verify whether any published case, cohort or trial demonstrates pseudo-Bartter caused by lipedema or occurring after lipedema liposuction. Do not infer a mechanism from an isolated postoperative potassium fall when bicarbonate, chloride, magnesium, renal indices, urine studies, blood pressure and RAAS were not measured. Include primary nephrology reviews and cases, official laboratory or guideline sources and relevant pharmacology labels; provide PMID, DOI, URLs and opened-source status. Search Spanish and European sources where available. Separate direct lipedema evidence, adjacent clinical evidence, mechanistic inference, anecdote and marketing. Treat eating-disorder or diuretic-misuse claims as hypotheses requiring evidence, never as conclusions from a laboratory pattern. End with a safe, simple explanation in Spanish, explicit limits and what a clinician would need to evaluate; provide no self-diagnosis algorithm, home treatment, potassium/salt/fluid instructions or dosing. Preserve artifacts and document inaccessible sources or terminal failures.
